# Autoimmune hemolytic anemia

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Hematology and oncology > Red blood cell disorders > Autoimmune hemolytic anemia*

[Original Article Link](/library/-H0DGh)

---

## Summary

Autoimmune <u>hemolytic anemias</u> (AIHAs) are a collection of disorders characterized by the destruction of <u>RBCs</u> through <u>antibody-mediated hemolysis</u> (extravascular and/or <u>intravascular</u>). There are two broad types, categorized by the temperature at which the <u>antigen</u>-<u>antibody</u> reactions maximally occur: <u>cold agglutinin hemolytic anemia</u> (<u>cold AIHA</u>) and <u>warm agglutinin hemolytic anemia</u> (<u>warm AIHA</u>). AIHAs can be either <u>idiopathic</u> or secondary to another disease e.g., infectious, lymphoproliferative, or autoimmune diseases. <u>Cold AIHA</u> and <u>warm AIHA</u> share some characteristics, e.g., they can both present with clinical <u>signs of anemia</u> and <u>laboratory signs of hemolysis</u>, and produce <u>symptomatic anemia</u> severe enough to require <u>blood transfusion</u>. However, their pathophysiology, etiology, <u>epidemiology</u>, clinical and diagnostic features, and targeted treatments all have key differences. Careful clinical and diagnostic evaluation (including <u>direct Coombs testing</u>, <u>antibody</u> <u>titers</u>, and <u>peripheral blood smear</u>) can help distinguish between the types, however, occasionally patients may have a mixed-type AIHA or unusual clinical presentations and laboratory findings. Management depends on the clinical presentation, etiology, and subtype, and is typically performed in consultation with a hematologist. Treatments include stabilization with <u>blood transfusion</u> and temporizing measures (e.g., <u>plasmapheresis</u>, plasma exchange), <u>systemic immunomodulators</u> (e.g., <u>glucocorticoids</u>, <u>rituximab</u>), treatment of underlying conditions, <u>supportive care</u>, and in <u>warm AIHA</u>, <u>splenectomy</u>.

---

## Overview

* Both <u>cold AIHA</u> and <u>warm AIHA</u>:

* Are <u>antibody</u>-mediated

* Can present with <u>signs of anemia</u>,

* Can show <u>laboratory signs of hemolysis</u>

* Are acutely treated with <u>blood transfusion</u> for <u>symptomatic anemia</u>

* Patients may occasionally exhibit a mixed-type AIHA or have atypical clinical presentations and initial diagnostic results. [[2]](/library/5mciT10)

* <u>Hematology</u> consultation is advised if the diagnosis is uncertain.

> [!TIP]
> Typical biochemical findings in <u>hemolysis</u> include ↓ <u>haptoglobin</u>, ↑ <u>LDH</u> concentration, ↑ <u>indirect bilirubin</u> concentration, <u>peripheral blood smear</u> abnormalities (e.g., ↑ <u>reticulocytes</u>, <u>schistocytes</u>, <u>spherocytes</u>, <u>polychromasia</u>), and <u>urinalysis</u> abnormalities (e.g., <u>hemoglobinuria</u>, <u>hemosiderinuria</u>, and <u>urobilinogen</u>).

## Cold agglutinin hemolytic anemia

### Background [[4]](/library/tIbXeE)[[5]](/library/EIb8eE)[[6]](/library/vIbAeE)




* Definitions: <u>Cold agglutinin hemolytic anemia</u> (<u>cold AIHA</u>) refers to a group of autoimmune disorders characterized by <u>hemolysis</u> that is caused by the binding of cold-sensitive <u>autoantibodies</u> to <u>RBCs</u> [[5]](/library/EIb8eE)[[7]](/library/VQXGEB)

* Cold agglutinin disease (<u>CAD</u>): a primary (<u>idiopathic</u>) form of <u>cold AIHA</u> in which <u>hemolysis</u> is mediated by monoclonal cold-sensitive <u>IgM</u> <u>autoantibodies</u> produced by a low-grade clonal <u>B-cell</u> <u>lymphoproliferative disorder</u> of the <u>bone marrow</u>

* Cold agglutinin syndrome (<u>CAS</u>): a rare form of <u>cold AIHA</u> in which cold-sensitive <u>autoantibody</u>-mediated <u>hemolysis</u> occurs secondary to another condition (e.g., infection, <u>lymphoma</u>)

* <u>Epidemiology</u> [[8]](/library/DIb1UE)

* <u>Cold AIHAs</u> comprise ∼ 10–25% of all AIHAs. [[2]](/library/5mciT10)[[7]](/library/VQXGEB)

* Most common in individuals > 50 years of age [[2]](/library/5mciT10)[[9]](/library/wIbhUE)





### Pathophysiology [[5]](/library/EIb8eE)




* Cold-sensitive antibodies (<u>cold agglutinins</u>): mostly <u>IgM antibodies</u> cause <u>extravascular hemolysis</u> and acute <u>intravascular hemolysis</u> 

* Stable disease: <u>extravascular hemolysis</u> of <u>complement</u>-coated <u>RBCs</u> by the <u>mononuclear phagocyte system</u>

* Acute exacerbations: <u>Intravascular hemolysis</u> can occur, mediated through the <u>complement system</u>, which is activated by <u>IgM antibodies</u> bound to <u>RBCs</u>.

* The <u>antigen</u>-<u>antibody</u> reaction is triggered by low body temperature and/or cold ambient temperatures.  [[5]](/library/EIb8eE)





### Etiology [[5]](/library/EIb8eE)




* <u>CAD</u>: <u>idiopathic</u>

* <u>CAS</u> occurs secondary to other diseases, including:

* <u>Mycoplasma</u> pneumoniae or <u>EBV</u> infection

* <u>Malignancy</u> (e.g., <u>non-Hodgkin lymphoma</u>, <u>CLL</u>)

* <u>Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia</u>





> [!NOTE]
> Cold weather is MMMMiserable: Cold (IgM) AIHA is seen in Malignancy (<u>CLL</u>), Mycoplasma <u>pneumonia</u>, and Mononucleosis.




### Clinical features




* Classically associated with cold exposure

* Can occur as episodes of acute, severe symptoms [[2]](/library/5mciT10)

* <u>Pallor</u>, fatigue, <u>weakness</u>

* Painful <u>cyanosis</u> of the extremities (<u>acrocyanosis</u>)

* <u>Livedo reticularis</u>

* <u>Raynaud phenomenon</u>

* <u>Skin</u> <u>ulcerations</u>





### Diagnostics [[5]](/library/EIb8eE)[[7]](/library/VQXGEB)[[10]](/library/hiXcrB)




* Indications for testing: typical cold-induced symptoms (e.g., <u>acrocyanosis</u>, <u>livedo reticularis</u>) or unexplained <u>anemia</u>

* Initial investigations: <u>CBC</u>, <u>reticulocyte count</u>, <u>hemolysis workup</u>, <u>DAT</u>, and <u>cold agglutinin</u> <u>titer</u>

* Additional investigations are indicated to identify secondary causes (i.e., to confirm <u>CAS</u>), for example:

* <u>Bone marrow biopsy</u> and <u>flow cytometry</u> of <u>bone marrow aspirate</u>

* <u>Serum protein electrophoresis</u>

* Workup for infectious diseases or <u>malignancy</u>, e.g., imaging, microbiology

* See also “<u>Antibody-mediated hemolysis</u>.”

* Diagnostics of <u>cold AIHA</u> can be established in patients with all of the following:

* <u>Evidence of hemolytic anemia</u>

* Direct <u>coombs test</u> (<u>DAT</u>): Indicates that the patient's <u>RBCs</u> are coated with <u>autoantibodies</u> and/or <u>complement</u> that are causing <u>hemolysis</u>

* <u>DAT</u> positive for C3d

* May also be weakly positive for <u>IgG</u>

* <u>Cold agglutinin</u> <u>titer</u> ≥ 64 at 4Â°C

* Other potential diagnostic findings (nonspecific)

* <u>PBS</u>: agglutination of <u>RBCs</u>; <u>spherocytes</u> may be seen

* ↓ C3 and C4 due to <u>complement</u> activation





> [!TIP]
> <u>Spherocytes</u> may be seen in both <u>cold AIHA</u> and <u>warm AIHA</u>. However, abundant <u>spherocytosis</u> is characteristic of <u>warm AIHA</u>.




![Agglutination of erythrocytes](media/tus66bfmf4pftm5aj7t0hr1c.jpg)

Agglutination of erythrocytes




### Management [[6]](/library/vIbAeE)[[10]](/library/hiXcrB)[[11]](/library/dQXoEB)




#### Approach




The goal is to reduce cold-induced symptoms, control <u>hemolysis</u>, and improve <u>anemia</u>. <u>Hematology</u> consult is advised.




* Compensated <u>hemolysis</u> and mild or absent circulatory symptoms : close surveillance

* Significant clinical manifestations: Start acute therapy.

* <u>CAD</u>: Consider chronic therapy (systemic immunomodulatory).

* <u>CAS</u>: Treat the underlying condition

* Advise all patients to avoid exposure to the cold.

* Consider <u>folic acid</u> DOSAGE supplementation in all patients.

* Manage disease complications: <u>Venous thromboembolism</u> (<u>VTE</u>) [[12]](/library/LoYwcJ)





> [!TIP]
> Spontaneous remission is rare in <u>CAD</u> but is common in <u>CAS</u> secondary to infection (e.g., <u>Mycoplasma</u>) and typically occurs within a few weeks of onset. [[5]](/library/EIb8eE)[[7]](/library/VQXGEB)




#### Acute therapy




* Indications: Severe <u>symptoms of anemia</u> or <u>Hb</u> < 7 g/dL

* Management

* <u>RBC</u> <u>transfusions</u> as needed

* Consider temporizing measures.

* <u>Plasmapheresis</u>

* Trial of <u>glucocorticoids</u>: e.g., <u>prednisolone</u> DOSAGE (however, the response is often poor)

* Consider <u>VTE prophylaxis</u> in patients with acute exacerbations of <u>hemolysis</u>.  [[7]](/library/VQXGEB)[[11]](/library/dQXoEB)





#### Long-term therapy




* Indications: <u>CAD</u> with either <u>symptomatic anemia</u> or significant cold-induced symptoms

* Treatment: <u>Systemic immunomodulators</u> 

* First-line treatment: <u>rituximab</u>  DOSAGE (anti-<u>CD20</u> <u>antibody</u>)  [[6]](/library/vIbAeE)

* Combination therapy (i.e., <u>rituximab</u> PLUS <u>bendamustine</u> OR <u>fludarabine</u>) is often recommended in severe disease.   [[6]](/library/vIbAeE)[[11]](/library/dQXoEB)





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Splenectomy</u> is not recommended for <u>cold AIHA</u>. It is not effective as most <u>extravascular hemolysis</u> occurs in the <u>liver</u>.

## Warm agglutinin hemolytic anemia

### Background [[6]](/library/vIbAeE)[[8]](/library/DIb1UE)[[13]](/library/ooY01J)[[14]](/library/KoYU1J)




* Definition: an autoimmune disease characterized by the binding of heat-sensitive <u>autoantibodies</u> to <u>RBCs</u>, which leads to the <u>phagocytosis</u> and destruction of <u>RBCs</u> in the <u>reticuloendothelial system</u> [[14]](/library/KoYU1J)

* <u>Epidemiology</u> [[15]](/library/0jXe_B)

* <u>Incidence</u>: 1–3 cases/100,000 individuals

* Can occur at any age





### Pathophysiology [[16]](/library/crbaTE)




* Heat-sensitive <u>antibodies</u>: Mostly polyclonal <u>IgG antibodies</u>;  that first bind to multiple <u>RBC</u> <u>antigens</u>, then to <u>Fc receptors</u> on <u>phagocytes</u>

* Binding of the <u>antibodies</u> leads to ↑ <u>extravascular hemolysis</u> mediated by the <u>reticuloendothelial system</u> of the <u>spleen</u> and <u>liver</u>.  [[16]](/library/crbaTE)

* The <u>antigen</u>-<u>antibody</u> reaction is triggered by body temperatures of â¥ 37.0Â°C (â¥ 98.6Â°F)





> [!NOTE]
> “Warm weather is Great”: Warm AIHA is IgG mediated.




### Etiology




* Mostly <u>idiopathic</u>

* Secondary causes

* <u>Malignancy</u> (<u>lymphoma</u>, <u>chronic lymphocytic leukemia</u>)

* Autoimmune diseases (e.g., <u>SLE</u>)

* Certain drugs (e.g., <u>rifampin</u>, <u>phenytoin</u>, <u>penicillins</u>, α-<u>methyldopa</u>) [[17]](/library/GlYBy6)





### Clinical features




* Symptom onset is typically gradual.

* <u>Signs of anemia</u> (<u>pallor</u>, fatigue, <u>weakness</u>)

* Mild <u>splenomegaly</u>





### Diagnostics [[11]](/library/dQXoEB)




* Initial investigations

* Order <u>CBC</u>, <u>reticulocyte count</u>, <u>hemolysis workup</u>, <u>DAT</u>, and <u>PBS</u>.

* Consider <u>warm AIHA</u> in patients with:

* <u>Laboratory evidence of hemolysis</u>

* <u>DAT</u> positive for <u>IgG</u> ± C3d not attributable to another cause (i.e., a recent <u>transfusion</u> or <u>cold agglutinin</u>)

* <u>PBS</u>: abundant <u>spherocytes</u>

* Difficulty findings <u>crossmatch</u>-compatible blood units for <u>transfusion</u>

* Additional investigations: to rule out secondary causes (see “<u>Antibody-mediated hemolysis</u>.”)





> [!TIP]
> Consider <u>warm AIHA</u> in patients with <u>severe anemia</u> for whom the blood bank is unable to find <u>crossmatch</u>-compatible blood units.




![Spherocytosis](media/qmm3gmt8boum1yp5wzwlzihh.jpg)

Spherocytosis




### Management  [[6]](/library/vIbAeE)[[11]](/library/dQXoEB)[[15]](/library/0jXe_B)




#### Approach




The goal is to control <u>hemolysis</u> and improve <u>anemia</u>. Early specialist consultation is advised (e.g., <u>hematology</u>, intensive care).




* Manage severe disease acutely.

* Address potential secondary causes (see “Etiology”).  [[18]](/library/2jXT-B)

* Hold any potentially causative medications.

* Identify and manage underlying conditions.

* Consider the need for chronic <u>systemic immunomodulators</u>.

* Observation without <u>immunosuppressive</u> interventions may be appropriate for patients with mild asymptomatic <u>anemia</u>.

* Manage disease complications: e.g., <u>VTE</u>

* Monitor for relapses and consider repeated therapeutic intervention.





#### Acute therapy




* Indications: Severe <u>symptoms of anemia</u> or <u>Hb</u> 6–7 g/dL

* Management

* Provide hemodynamic and <u>respiratory support</u> as needed.

* Alert the blood bank early about the need for a <u>transfusion</u> in a patient with <u>warm agglutinin hemolytic anemia</u>.  [[15]](/library/0jXe_B)

* Consider an <u>RBC</u> <u>transfusion</u> under specialist guidance.  [[6]](/library/vIbAeE)[[15]](/library/0jXe_B)[[19]](/library/u5XpNA)

* Consider temporizing measures.

* Early treatment with high-dose <u>glucocorticoids</u> (e.g., <u>methylprednisolone</u> DOSAGE)

* <u>Rescue therapy</u> with IVIG DOSAGE or plasma exchange

* Consider <u>VTE prophylaxis</u> in patients with acute exacerbations of <u>hemolysis</u>.  [[11]](/library/dQXoEB)





> [!WARNING]
> Do not delay a potentially life-saving <u>blood transfusion</u> in unstable patients with <u>severe anemia</u>, even if <u>crossmatched</u> blood is unavailable. Use type-specific uncrossmatched blood in close consultation with the blood bank. [[15]](/library/0jXe_B)




#### Long-term therapy




* Indications: Consider in most patients to reduce <u>autoantibody</u> production.

* Treatment: typically involves <u>systemic immunomodulators</u> 

* First-line: high-dose <u>glucocorticoids</u>

* Second-line: <u>rituximab</u>

* Third-line: <u>steroid</u>-sparing <u>immunosuppressants</u> or <u>splenectomy</u>





References: [[6]](/library/vIbAeE)[[8]](/library/DIb1UE)[[13]](/library/ooY01J)[[14]](/library/KoYU1J)
